title: Cyclic Vector Theorem: Full Biconditional
description: Proves the converse direction of the cyclic vector theorem: if M has a cyclic vector then M is nonderogatory (minpoly = charpoly). Combined with the parent theorem (nonderogatory → cyclic vector), this gives the full biconditional: IsNonderogatory M ↔ ∃ v, IsCyclicVector M v. Fully machine-verified: 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

meta.author: Lean Genius Research
meta.assumptions: No axioms or sorries. Uses only Mathlib's Polynomial and Matrix APIs.
originalContributions: cyclic_implies_nonderogatory: proves the converse direction — if M has a cyclic vector v then minpoly K M = M.charpoly
nonderogatory_iff_has_cyclic_vector: full biconditional combining parent and converse directions
derogatory_has_no_cyclic_vector: contrapositive — a derogatory matrix has no cyclic vector
minpoly_natDegree_of_cyclic: degree characterization — a matrix with a cyclic vector has deg(minpoly) = n
meta.historicalContext: The cyclic vector theorem is a cornerstone of rational canonical form (RCF) theory, traceable to Frobenius's 1878 work on the elementary divisors of matrices and Hilbert's 1888 algebraic invariants. The forward direction (nonderogatory ⟹ cyclic vector) was proved in the parent entry using primary decomposition over arbitrary fields. The converse direction settled here completes the characterization: a matrix is nonderogatory if and only if it has a cyclic vector. This biconditional is the key step in showing that every nonderogatory matrix is similar to its companion matrix, and thus that the rational canonical form is unique up to ordering of invariant factors. Standard textbook treatments (Hoffman–Kunze, Dummit–Foote, Roman) state this biconditional as a single result; the formal split into forward and converse directions is dictated by Lean's separation of concerns.
meta.proofStrategy: Given a cyclic vector v for M, we show deg(minpoly K M) = n by a degree squeeze: (1) minpoly | charpoly via Cayley-Hamilton, giving deg ≤ n; (2) if deg < n, the cyclic condition forces minpoly = 0, contradicting ne_zero, giving deg ≥ n. Then both minpoly and charpoly are monic of the same degree with minpoly | charpoly, forcing equality.

overview.problemStatement:
**Open question from cayley-hamilton-cyclic-vector-all-fields**: Is the cyclic vector theorem an equivalence? The parent theorem shows every nonderogatory matrix has a cyclic vector. Does the converse hold — if $M$ has a cyclic vector, must $M$ be nonderogatory?

More precisely: does
$$\text{IsNonderogatory}(M) \iff \exists v,\ \text{IsCyclicVector}(M, v)$$
hold over any field $K$?
overview.historicalContext: A matrix $M \in K^{n \times n}$ is **nonderogatory** if its minimal polynomial $\mu_M$ equals its characteristic polynomial $\chi_M$. Equivalently, $\dim_K K[M] = n$ — the algebra generated by $M$ has the maximum possible dimension. The **cyclic vector theorem** states that every nonderogatory matrix has a *cyclic vector*: a vector $v$ such that $\{v, Mv, M^2 v, \dots, M^{n-1} v\}$ is a basis of $K^n$. The converse is also classical: if $v$ is cyclic for $M$, then the evaluation map $p \mapsto p(M) \cdot v$ gives a $K[X]$-module isomorphism $K[X]/(\mu_M) \cong K^n$, forcing $\dim_K K[X]/(\mu_M) = n$, hence $\deg \mu_M = n = \deg \chi_M$, hence $\mu_M = \chi_M$. The classical proof goes via module isomorphisms; the Lean formalization here uses a more elementary degree-squeeze argument that avoids constructing the isomorphism explicitly. This biconditional is what ultimately justifies the *rational canonical form*: every matrix is similar to a block-diagonal matrix of companion matrices, and a matrix is similar to a *single* companion matrix if and only if it is nonderogatory.
keyInsights: A cyclic vector forces deg(minpoly) ≥ n: if deg < n, the cyclic condition (IsCyclicVector M v) requires that any nonzero p of degree < n with $p(M) \cdot v = 0$ must be zero — but minpoly(M) = 0 as a matrix, giving a contradiction unless deg(minpoly) ≥ n.

Both minpoly and charpoly are monic of degree n with minpoly | charpoly. Extracting the quotient r = charpoly / minpoly and using degree arithmetic shows deg(r) = 0, forcing r monic of degree 0, hence r = 1.

The final step uses Polynomial.Monic.of_mul_monic_left to deduce that r is monic (since both minpoly and charpoly are monic and the product equals charpoly), then Polynomial.eq_C_of_natDegree_eq_zero to write r = C(r.coeff 0) = C(1) = 1.

The biconditional nonderogatory_iff_has_cyclic_vector trivially combines cyclic_implies_nonderogatory with nonderogatory_has_cyclic_vector from the parent entry — but this combination encodes a deep structural equivalence between an algebraic property (μ = χ) and a geometric property (a single vector spans K[M]·v).

The contrapositive formulation (derogatory ⟹ no cyclic vector) is computationally useful: to certify that a matrix is derogatory, exhibit any vector for which the iterated images fail to be linearly independent — even one such v is enough to rule out cyclic-vector existence by the biconditional.

Over any field — including finite fields F_q with q ≤ n — the biconditional holds without hypothesis on field size. This is the field-independence that the parent entry's title emphasizes ('all fields'), inherited automatically by the biconditional formed here.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Step 1 (deg ≤ n)**: minpoly K M divides M.charpoly by Cayley-Hamilton (`minpoly.dvd` applied to `Matrix.aeval_self_charpoly`), so $\text{natDegree}(\mu_M) \leq \text{natDegree}(\chi_M) = n$.

**Step 2 (deg ≥ n)**: Suppose $\text{natDegree}(\mu_M) < n$. Then $\text{aeval}\,M\,(\mu_M) = 0$ as a matrix, so $(\text{aeval}\,M\,\mu_M) \cdot v = 0$. But IsCyclicVector M v requires this to imply $\mu_M = 0$ — contradicting `minpoly.ne_zero (Matrix.isIntegral M)`.

**Step 3 (equality)**: $\text{natDegree}(\mu_M) = n$. Write $\chi_M = \mu_M \cdot r$. Both sides monic of degree n: $\deg(r) = 0$, $r$ monic, so $r = 1$ and $\chi_M = \mu_M$.
prerequisites: minpoly.dvd: the minimal polynomial divides any annihilating polynomial (applied to Cayley-Hamilton)
minpoly.aeval: aeval M (minpoly K M) = 0 as a matrix
Polynomial.Monic.of_mul_monic_left: if p·q is monic and p is monic, then q is monic
Polynomial.eq_C_of_natDegree_eq_zero: a polynomial of degree 0 equals C(coeff 0)
openQuestions: Does the biconditional extend to matrices over commutative rings (not just fields)? The proof crucially uses that K[X] is a PID to extract the quotient r and that minpoly is well-defined for integral elements. Over a general commutative ring, neither holds in general, and the cyclic-vector theorem fails: even simple examples like $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ exhibit obstructions.

Can the converse be used to give a shorter proof of the rational canonical form theorem? The biconditional shows nonderogatory matrices are 'as good as' companion matrices. A clean RCF proof would: (1) decompose $K^n$ as $K[X]$-module into cyclic submodules (invariant-factor decomposition), (2) on each cyclic summand apply the biconditional to get a companion-matrix block, (3) assemble.

Is there a computationally efficient algorithm to *find* a cyclic vector when one exists? The proof in the parent file is constructive (via primary decomposition) but expensive. Probabilistic algorithms (Eberly 1991, Storjohann 1998) find a cyclic vector for nonderogatory matrices in $\tilde{O}(n^\omega)$ field operations with high probability — formalizing such an algorithm in Lean 4 would be a substantial project.

sections.title: Header: Statement and Proof Outline
sections.summary: Documents the converse direction (cyclic vector ⟹ nonderogatory) and lays out the four-step proof strategy: (1) Cayley–Hamilton gives μ | χ, (2) cyclicity forces deg μ ≥ n, (3) divisibility + equal degrees + monic forces μ = χ. The header also notes the file's status: 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

sections.title: Main Converse: cyclic_implies_nonderogatory
sections.summary: Proves IsCyclicVector M v ⟹ IsNonderogatory M (i.e., μ_M = χ_M). The proof squeezes deg(μ_M) between n (from below, via cyclicity + minpoly.aeval) and n (from above, via Cayley–Hamilton + divisibility). With both polynomials monic of degree n and one dividing the other, equality follows by extracting the quotient r and showing r = 1.

sections.title: Corollary: derogatory_has_no_cyclic_vector
sections.summary: Contrapositive of cyclic_implies_nonderogatory: a derogatory matrix (¬IsNonderogatory) has no cyclic vector. Useful for exhibiting non-cyclicity by ruling out IsNonderogatory.

sections.title: Degree Characterization: minpoly_natDegree_of_cyclic
sections.summary: A matrix with a cyclic vector has natDegree(minpoly) = n. Follows from cyclic_implies_nonderogatory + Matrix.charpoly_natDegree_eq_dim. Provides a numerical invariant useful for computational checks of cyclicity.

conclusion.summary: The full biconditional `IsNonderogatory M ↔ ∃ v, IsCyclicVector M v` is now machine-verified over arbitrary fields in Lean 4. The converse direction proves that a cyclic vector forces the minimal polynomial to have degree n, completing the characterization of nonderogatory matrices. The proof avoids constructing the explicit $K[X]/(\mu_M) \cong K^n$ module isomorphism (which is the textbook approach), using instead a direct degree-squeeze that lifts cleanly to Lean's polynomial API.
conclusion.implications: This completes the cyclic vector characterization of nonderogatory matrices in Mathlib-compatible Lean 4. The biconditional is the key step connecting nonderogatory matrices to companion matrices in rational canonical form theory: a matrix is similar to a single companion matrix if and only if it has a cyclic vector. The contrapositive (derogatory ⟹ no cyclic vector) provides a clean obstruction theorem useful in module-theoretic arguments. The degree characterization gives a computational test: cyclicity is equivalent to $\deg \mu_M = n$, which can be checked in polynomial time via Smith normal form. Together with the parent file's primary-decomposition proof of the forward direction, this gives a complete formal account of the cyclic-vector theorem over arbitrary fields, including finite fields where naive 'open dense set' arguments fail.
openQuestions: Extend to modules over commutative Noetherian rings (not just fields). The proof crucially uses that $K[X]$ is a PID and that minpoly is well-defined; over a general commutative ring, both can fail.
Use the biconditional to give a shorter rational canonical form existence proof: decompose $K^n$ as $K[X]$-module, apply the biconditional to each cyclic summand, assemble into block-diagonal form.

Formalize a probabilistic algorithm (Eberly 1991, Storjohann 1998) that finds a cyclic vector for a nonderogatory matrix in $\tilde{O}(n^\omega)$ field operations — turning the existence theorem into a computational tool.
